Egypt reopens its embassy in Tripoli after twelve years, and uses the occasion to challenge the Libya-Turkey maritime deal

Cairo reopened its embassy in Tripoli on Saturday, 7 November, after it had been shut since 2014. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty used the ceremony to tell Libyan Prime Minister Dbeibah that Egypt's concerns about the Turkey-Libya maritime agreement must count [1][3].

On Saturday, 7 November 2026, Egypt reopened its embassy in Tripoli, closed since 2014: a closure of twelve years according to Reuters and most outlets, while Al Jazeera mentions eight years in a caption [2][3].
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty arrived in Libya the same day and inaugurated the mission's headquarters [3].
At the embassy he met Libya's acting oil minister and pushed to speed up gas pipeline projects and the refining of Libyan crude in Egypt [1].

Abdelatty told Prime Minister Dbeibah that Cairo's concerns should be taken into account when maritime boundaries are drawn; Dbeibah replied that his government would discuss the maritime delimitation file with Egypt [1].
The Libyan prime minister then mentioned a joint Libyan-Egyptian committee, whose next meeting would be held in Tripoli or Cairo [1].

On 20 October, the House of Representatives, the eastern parliament aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar, ratified the memorandum signed in 2019 between Turkey and the former Government of National Accord in Tripoli. Egypt, a longtime backer of Haftar, rejects the deal [1][5].
Saddam Haftar presented the deal as a tool to protect Libya's economic interests, while the Tripoli government's Foreign Ministry sees it as a "positive development" for relations with Turkey [1].
Key point: by reopening its embassy in Tripoli, Egypt, long turned toward eastern Libya, also opens a channel to the western government just as a Turkish maritime deal troubles it [1][3].

The link is direct: the deal ratified on 20 October draws a maritime zone between Turkey and Libya that Egypt and Cyprus reject. The European Union says it violates the rights of third states, and Greek officials argue the 2020 Egypt-Greece agreement effectively voids it [1].

The paradox is that the text was ratified by the eastern parliament, the one Cairo backs. Egypt can therefore no longer rely on its eastern allies alone: it has to talk to both Libyan camps, which Al Jazeera reads as a sign of regional shift on Libya [1][2].

Behind the diplomacy lie resources: gas, pipelines, crude to be refined in Egypt [1]. Delimiting maritime zones decides who can explore for and produce hydrocarbons in the eastern Mediterranean: a line on a map becomes an issue of energy and revenue.

If you live in Europe, Libya matters to you through Mediterranean gas and oil, migration routes and tensions between Greece, Turkey and their neighbours. Nothing changes at the pump or on your bill for now: this is a diplomatic step, worth watching if talks on maritime borders advance or if a compromise calms the dispute.

South Africa
South Africa: the ANC stays first in local elections with 30.8%, but the DA takes the big cities and everything will hinge on coalitions

Final results of the 4 November local elections give the ANC 30.76% of the vote and the DA 24.64%, far from any majority. The number of hung councils rises to 142 according to the Mail & Guardian, against 70 in 2021, and parties have 14 days to form alliances [3][5].

South Africans voted on 4 November 2026 to renew their municipal councils; the Electoral Commission (IEC) declared the final results on Sunday, 8 November, through its chairman Mosotho Moepya, who judged the vote free and fair [3].
The African National Congress (ANC) comes first with 30.76% of the vote and 3,246 council seats; the Democratic Alliance (DA) gets 24.64% and 1,695 seats, and ActionSA 5.67% and 313 seats [6].
Turnout reaches 52%, against 45.9% in the 2021 local elections, and 14.9 million voters cast ballots [3][6].
The ANC controls only 53 municipalities outright and remains the leading party in 128; hung councils rise to 142 according to the Mail & Guardian (the Witness counts 139), against 70 in 2021 [3][6].

In the near-complete count relayed by Reuters, Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party comes third with about 10% of the vote, and the DA leads in Johannesburg with about 35% against 20% for the ANC [5].

According to the Daily Maverick, the DA now leads the ANC in the three Gauteng metros where the ANC came first in 2021; in Nelson Mandela Bay the DA has 53 of 120 seats against 32 for the ANC, and in eThekwini (Durban) the ANC drops to 37 seats [4].

Parties have 14 days after the final declaration to negotiate. ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula called the result "catastrophic" but said his party would not go begging for positions; the ANC will sit in opposition if the terms of a coalition do not suit it [5].

Key point: the ANC remains the country's first party but loses its grip on the big cities, and coalition negotiations, more than the ballot box, will now decide who runs Johannesburg, Tshwane or Durban [4][5].

Reuters notes that the ANC's share has fallen from one local election to the next for fifteen years, largely because of failures in basic services such as water and electricity [5]. That is where the municipal vote is most concrete, since councils run these services.

The mechanism is that of hung councils: when no party holds more than half the seats, a deal is needed to elect the mayor and pass the budget. Analysts see an ANC-DA alliance as the most stable option in Johannesburg, mirroring their arrangement at national level [5]. But ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba openly opposes Helen Zille, whose name is circulating for the Johannesburg mayoralty [4].

DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis has prepared transparent coalition frameworks and is considering a "government of local unity" model for hung councils; the SACP, for its part, has invited the ANC, EFF, MK and other "left" parties to discuss alliances [7].

If you have ties to South Africa (travel, family, investments), remember that the stability of the big cities is being decided in these negotiations: local water, electricity and transport depend on it. For a reader in France, the effect is indirect: a fragile coalition slows reforms and weighs on investor confidence in one of the continent's major economies. Nothing changes in your daily life in the short term.

Nigeria: the Dangote refinery IPO draws three times more money than planned, but the deal is not yet wrapped up

According to sources cited by Reuters, the $1.6 billion offering for Dangote's refinery in Lagos has received orders of 6.4 trillion naira ($4.78 billion), nearly three times the target. Regulatory approval and the listing are still to come [1][2].

The public offering for the Dangote refinery in Lagos opened on 14 September and closed on 27 October 2026, according to the offer's official website, which says applications are still being checked [6].
The regulator (SEC) set the price at 525 naira per share, about $0.40; the base offering is about 2.15 trillion naira (about $1.6 billion) and 4.1 billion new shares [3][7].
That represents about 3.3% of the refinery's enlarged capital after the operation: far from a sale of control [7].
According to sources cited by Reuters, orders reach 6.4 trillion naira ($4.78 billion), about three times the target, mostly from Nigerian investors, retail and institutional [1][2].
An over-allotment option ("greenshoe") could raise the deal to as much as $2.1 billion; one source told Reuters that Dangote was expected to exercise it, but the company has not confirmed [1].

According to the press, the regulator is aiming for 17 November for its approval, and listing on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) is expected in late November or early December, subject to approval [1][5].

The group is also preparing a 700,000-barrel-a-day refinery in Lamu, Kenya, a $16 billion project whose groundbreaking took place in September in the presence of Kenyan President Ruto and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed; a Kenyan tribunal dismissed a consumer association's petition against the project [8][9].
Key point: Nigeria's biggest IPO draws about three times more money than planned, showing local savers' appetite for an industrial project presented as national, but the deal is not finished [1][2].

A refinery turns crude oil into fuels. Producing them locally avoids importing them, which affects pump prices and the country's foreign-currency reserves: this is why the IPO goes beyond finance alone.

Only 3.3% of the capital is offered: the deal opens the refinery to individual investors without giving up control [7]. The price is set at 525 naira, and it is demand that will show, from the first trading sessions, whether that price holds against the market; demand before listing does not predict the price after [3].

The deal is part of the group's expansion toward East Africa, with the Lamu project in Kenya, where the local tribunal has set aside a first challenge [8][9]. The timetable still depends on the regulator's green light, expected around 17 November according to the press [5].

If you are in France, this stock is not easy to access: the offer is aimed first at Nigerian investors. But a Nigeria that refines more of its own oil imports less fuel, and new African refineries are gradually changing the flows of oil products. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

news.2026-11-09-gambie-presidentielle-be: Gambia: less than a month before the presidential election, Talib Ahmed Bensouda's candidacy is challenged by the government

The Gambia votes on 5 December to elect its president, and nominations run until 14 November. Talib Ahmed Bensouda, the Coalition 2026 candidate, has filed his papers while a government white paper casts doubt on his eligibility [1][2][3].
The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) receives nominations from 3 to 14 November, for a vote on 5 December 2026 [1][2].

Twenty-seven aspirants were initially on the list, including incumbent President Adama Barrow (NPP) and opposition figure Ousainou Darboe (UDP); at the halfway point, Alkali Cham had withdrawn, bringing the number of withdrawals to three [1].
On Saturday, Talib Ahmed Bensouda, a former mayor of Kanifing, filed his papers for Coalition 2026 [1][3].

A government white paper on a commission of inquiry into local government raises the possibility of barring him; Bensouda replies that his report contains "nothing that can stop" him from running [3].
If elected, he promises to introduce a two-term limit for presidents; his coalition announces a 66-point programme [4].
Key point: the campaign is first fought over the rules, that is, who is allowed to run, with which documents and what deposit, before the first rally [1][3].

This is the first presidential election under a revised electoral framework, which raises the thresholds for filing a candidacy and registering a party; the IEC requires original documents and proof of the deposit [1]. A dispute over eligibility can therefore weigh as much as a result at the ballot box; the IEC will publish the final list of candidates after vetting [1].
If you have ties to West Africa, note that this election in a small country surrounded by Senegal will be closely watched. Nothing changes for you in the short term.

Algeria
Algeria: the 2027 budget bets on a $60 barrel and a deficit of about 16% of GDP, ahead of the 16 November vote

Algerian lawmakers will vote on 16 November on the 2027 finance bill: 9,251 billion dinars in revenue against 17,882 billion in spending appropriations, a barrel fixed at $60 and growth of 4.2%. The deficit, of the order of 16% of GDP, is deduced by difference [2][4][5].

Finance Minister Mohamed Lamine Lebbou presented the text to the National People's Assembly (APN) on 2 November; the plenary vote is set for Monday, 16 November at 9 a.m., after which the text goes to the Council of the Nation and is due to take effect on 1 January 2027 [3][5].
Revenue is estimated at 9,251.1 billion dinars, against 8,611.1 billion expected in 2026, i.e. 7.4% more; payment appropriations reach 17,882.6 billion dinars, the equivalent of $132 billion [4].

The deficit, about 8,631.5 billion dinars (around $63 billion, against $71 billion in 2026), is not explicitly stated in the text: it is deduced from the difference between revenue and spending [2][4].
The assumptions used: growth of 4.2% in 2027, a reference oil price of $60 a barrel, average inflation of 4% and a rate of 131 dinars to the dollar over 2027-2029 [3][4].
The APN's finance committee proposes amendments; one would make any revision of fuel prices subject to Parliament's approval through the finance law [1][3].
Key point: the Algerian state spends almost twice what it collects, and its budget depends on oil and gas prices, hence the $60 reference barrel [4].

Former IMF adviser Abdelrahmi Bessaha calculates that revenue covers only 51.7% of spending in 2027 [6]. According to an economist cited by Maghreb Émergent, the deficit reaches 16.2% of GDP, against 12.4% announced for 2026, but these ratios are not comparable because the 2027 bill counts all appropriations; with the GDP used by the IMF, the same deficit would weigh 19.16% [2].

Algeria is a gas supplier to Europe and France: the soundness of its accounts depends on that market. Nothing changes in your daily life, but a budget that counts on gas and oil can also be read as a bet on their prices.
